capabilities.title: Verified simplification
capabilities.summary: Searches a short chain of rewrites toward a goal (simplify, expand, factor, or rewrite in given functions): handbook identities, each at every place it matches and read in either direction, plus SymPy's own moves. Every step is checked at random complex sample points and, separately, with a symbolic zero test; the steps and the identities used are shown. A result that cannot be verified is never shown.
limits: Numerical agreement at sample points is evidence, not proof; only a passed symbolic zero test means SymPy also reduced the difference to zero. Both are reported for every step.

Steps are equalities where both sides are defined. When the result excludes points the input did not (a cancelled factor), it says where it is valid (`x \neq 1`); square-root, logarithm and branch-cut domains are not reported this way.
The search is bounded (at most 4 rewrites in a row, a few alternatives per step, a time budget). "Nothing better was found" does not show that no better form exists.
An identity that matches but whose conditions are not provable from your assumptions is reported with the unmet conditions and never applied.
Symbols are complex unless you declare otherwise, so results that need real or positive symbols are left alone until you say so.
If nothing better is found, the input is returned unchanged and the status says so.
In LaTeX, bare function arguments such as `\sin 2x` and inverse notation such as `\sin^{-1}` are rejected as ambiguous; plain text needs the parentheses, `sin(2*x)`.

capabilities.title: Verified Taylor series
capabilities.summary: Expands an expression in one variable about a finite real point, to order 12 at most. The coefficients are re-derived from the original function by a contour-integral estimate (no differentiation), and the remainder is measured to shrink at the claimed order. Both checks must pass or no series is shown.
limits: Only Taylor series about a finite point. A pole or branch point at the point (`1/x`, `\sqrt{x}`, `\ln x` at 0) is "unsupported"; Laurent, Puiseux and asymptotic series are not produced.
Functions with no complex derivative (`|x|`) are unsupported.
The error table is a measurement at a few distances for this expression, not a bound.

capabilities.title: Noncommutative matrix calculus
capabilities.summary: Ordered products of matrix exponentials with declared matrices (a size, or explicit entries), also matrices that depend on a variable, A(t). Minerva recognises the structure and picks the technique: the ordered product rule; the Frechet derivative of exp(X(t)) when X and X' do not commute (never assumed to equal X' exp(X)); merging exponentials only where commutation is declared or visible in the entries; a closed form for an invertible matrix; Duhamel integrals of e^((t-s)A) B e^(sA); a Sylvester equation or a block-matrix exponential for other integrals; and evolution operators dU/dt = A(t) U, U(0) = I. A result is shown only if independent checks agree. An equation, a representation or a numerical approximation is never presented as an evaluated result.
limits: The variable is scalar. A matrix depends on it only if declared (or visible in explicit entries), and A(t) is never read as t times A; integrals of time-dependent matrices are not supported.
Matrices are never assumed to commute (also with their own derivative or at other times) or to be invertible; each must be declared, or be visible in explicit entries.

Time-ordered exponentials, Dyson series and Magnus expansions are not supported. An abstract generator that does not commute with itself at all times is declined; explicit entries with a numeric span are solved numerically.

A numerical solution (up to 4 by 4, double precision) is a measurement on the span you give, checked by a second method, by integrating backwards and by Liouville's formula; the end of the span is a number only you can choose.

Integrals need exponents that are affine in the variable and at most two exponentials depending on it. Abstract matrices give an exact equation or representation, entries only for explicit matrices (at most 4 by 4) whose closed form SymPy finds in time.
The numerical check is evidence, not proof. The exact check compares formal power series through degree 4 and is reported separately.

capabilities.title: Dirac delta and Heaviside calculus
capabilities.summary: Simplify, integrate and differentiate expressions with Dirac delta and Heaviside functions. Equality is as distributions (the same action on every test function), never pointwise: a delta has no values to compare. Each step cites a handbook identity and the conditions that were established exactly (the variable is real, a scale factor is nonzero, a root is real and simple, a delta lies inside the limits); a result is shown only if an independent test-function pairing against a regularised input agrees. Whatever cannot be decided is refused with a reason, never guessed.
limits: One real variable. A delta needs a polynomial argument with simple real roots; repeated roots, other functions (sin x) and products of distributions are declined.
A delta exactly on an integration limit counts only under a convention you choose (half, include or exclude); Minerva never picks one.

Heaviside functions are differentiated when the argument is affine and the other factors are smooth everywhere; derivatives of a delta, products of steps and integrals of ordinary functions with a step are declined.

The test-function check is supporting evidence, not a proof; the exact conditions are reported separately. Write `delta(x)` or `\delta(x)` (outside this operation they are ordinary symbols) and Minerva asks whether it is a Dirac delta, and `theta(x)` whether it is a step function, then computes nothing until you answer. The explicit names (\operatorname{DiracDelta}, \operatorname{Heaviside}) need no question.

capabilities.title: Differential geometry in coordinates
capabilities.summary: Give the coordinates and a metric once and ask for the inverse metric, the Christoffel symbols of the Levi-Civita connection, the Riemann, Ricci and Einstein tensors, the Ricci scalar and other curvature invariants, symbolic geodesic equations, and the covariant derivative or index raising of a tensor field. Functions of the coordinates (f(r), a(t)) may be declared. The conventions are stated with every result. A quantity is shown only if independent numerical checks pass: the connection is checked for metric compatibility, the curvature for its symmetries and the Bianchi identities, the Einstein tensor for a vanishing divergence, the geodesic equations against the Euler-Lagrange equations. A symbolic proof is reported separately, and the signature is never assumed.
limits: Explicit metrics only, in at most 4 coordinates, with real coordinates. No abstract manifolds, charts or atlases, tetrads, spin connections or differential forms; the connection is always Levi-Civita.
Unspecified functions are real functions of the coordinates; an undeclared f(r) is refused instead of being read as f times r.

The signature is reported only when the declared assumptions decide the sign of each entry of a diagonal metric. Where a determinant or denominator vanishes is reported as a restriction on the coordinates, not as a statement about curvature singularities; root, logarithm and branch domains are not analysed.
Numerical agreement is evidence, not proof. A symbolic proof (a zero test that succeeded) is shown separately and is not attempted for very large expressions.
Geodesic equations are symbolic; they are not integrated numerically.

capabilities.title: Identity search with applicability checks
capabilities.summary: Retrieval proposes handbook identities that may fit an expression. The engine then matches each pattern, checks its validity conditions against your declared assumptions, rewrites, and verifies the rewrite.
limits: An identity whose conditions cannot be proven from your assumptions is reported, with the unmet conditions, and not applied.
Matches that only work by inventing roots, reciprocals or the imaginary unit are discarded.
Retrieval is keyword and structure based; semantic search is planned.

capabilities.title: Derivations in the workbench
capabilities.summary: Builds a derivation step by step without a language model. Each step is an operation (simplify, differentiate, integrate, Taylor polynomial) or a handbook identity applied to the previous result, and is verified and saved to your account with what produced it and the assumptions in force. You can continue from any earlier step.
limits: A step is carried forward as its text form, which the parser reads back exactly. A result the text parser cannot read (for example one using `erf` or `Piecewise`) is shown but cannot be continued.

An identity is offered only when the engine reports it applicable (conditions proven from your assumptions); applying it recomputes and re-verifies the rewrite on the server. Handbook entries that are only stated are never applied.
If you edit a carried-forward result, the next step is recorded as a new input, not a continuation.

capabilities.title: Find the conserved quantities of a system
capabilities.summary: Give a Lagrangian or a Hamiltonian and ask for its conserved quantities. Minerva derives the equations of motion (confirmed by numerical differentiation), then searches a deterministic ladder of larger and larger families of candidates: polynomials in the velocities or momenta times powers of the coordinates, cos and sin of angles (declared, detected, or cyclic) and powers of t. In each family the conservation condition is solved exactly; a candidate is shown only if it is verified on the equations of motion, and products of what is already known are not counted as discoveries. It then reports which constants are functionally independent (an exact Jacobian rank, with the algebraic relations that tie the rest to them) and exactly which families were and were not searched. You do not choose an ansatz, a power bound or the angles.
limits: Complete within each family searched and nothing more. No additional constant always means within the explored families, never that the system has none.
Only rational equations of motion are searched. Square roots (Cartesian Kepler), logarithms and non-polynomial time dependence are reported as unsupported. At most 3 coordinates.
Families are capped (350 unknown coefficients by default); larger ones are listed as not searched.
Parameters are generic. Constants that exist only at special values (resonant frequency ratios) are found only when those values are given.
Functional independence is a proved lower bound (exact rank at rational points); it is called exact only when an upper bound from the relations meets it. Numerical sampling is never used as proof.
A name such as Runge–Lenz is a recognition the model may offer afterwards; the search never uses it.

capabilities.title: Search for hidden constants of motion
capabilities.summary: Looks for constants of motion beyond cyclic coordinates, energy and rotations, such as the Runge–Lenz vector of the Kepler problem. It solves exactly for every combination of functions of the coordinates (powers, and cos and sin of coordinates you declare to be angles) times velocity monomials of a chosen degree whose time derivative vanishes on the equations of motion. Only constants that pass the same verification as the others are shown, and the known ones and their products are left out of the count.
limits: It searches one declared family and says which. Finding nothing proves nothing outside that family.
Time-dependent Lagrangians, accelerations with square roots or other non-rational functions, and more than three coordinates are refused.
The family is capped (500 unknown coefficients); a bigger one is reported as a resource limit.
Naming a constant (for example as the Runge–Lenz vector) is a recognition the model may offer, not something the search proves.

limits: Entries recorded from the literature ("stated") carry no rule and are never used to rewrite anything.
Coverage is limited and growing; quantum field theory is stated entries only.

capabilities.title: Chat with a model you host
capabilities.summary: A conversation in which a language model plans, asks and explains, and calls the tools above. It runs only when you connect a model, such as one served by Ollama; it is off by default.
limits: The model never computes and never decides correctness. Formulas it writes that no tool produced in the conversation are shown as unchecked. Equations it writes are called false only when the sides differ by a constant; definitions, coordinate changes and equations of motion are not identities, stay unchecked, and are judged only against definitions stated earlier in the conversation.
How well it chooses tools depends on the model, and no model tried so far passes every evaluation case. See docs/model-evaluation.md.
Only Ollama-compatible hosts are supported.

capabilities.title: Read formulas from a photo
capabilities.summary: Attach a photo or screenshot of an equation in the chat. A vision model you host transcribes it to LaTeX, you confirm or correct the transcription, and Minerva's strict parser shows how it reads each formula before anything is computed. The model only transcribes; it never solves, simplifies or decides anything about the image.
limits: A transcription can be wrong, which is why you confirm it before it is used. Only what the parser accepts from the confirmed text is passed on to the tools.
Ambiguous notation is refused exactly as typed input is, for example `\sin 2x`.
Images are never stored or logged, and are limited in size to PNG, JPEG or WebP files.
It needs a vision-capable model on the Ollama-compatible host you connect.
